site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: A Promise Measured in Three Steps
body: When the generous asura king Bali held the celestial realm in his care, Lord Vishnu came among the gathered priests as the quiet young brahmana Vamana. At Bali's grand sacrifice, the small-seeming mendicant asked only for land that three of his steps could cover, and Bali, true to his nature, gave his word despite his teacher's worried counsel.

Then Vamana unfolded into a vast cosmic form, and with two gentle strides he spanned the radiant earth and the shining heaven of the gods. There was nowhere left for the third step, yet Bali did not waver. He bent low and offered his own head as the resting place, honoring the sacred vow he had spoken.

Moved by such steadfast honesty, Vishnu did not cast Bali down but blessed him instead, granting him the prosperous kingdom of Sutala and promising to keep watch at his side, while Indra joyfully received the celestial realm once more. Generosity, humility, and divine mercy met together that day and shone as one.

stories.title: A Friend's Welcome at Dvaraka
body: Sudama, a humble brahmana and old classmate of Krishna from the days with their teacher Sandipani, walked toward the shining city of Dvaraka carrying only a small bundle of parched rice. Encouraged by his wife, he had set out hoping simply to see his childhood friend again, with no expectation of reward.

From his royal seat, Krishna caught sight of Sudama in the distance, rose at once, and rushed to embrace him with the delight of a boy reunited with a dear companion. He personally honored his friend and, with warm joy, ate the plain rice as though it were the most precious offering imaginable.

Sudama never asked for a thing, content just to sit beside Krishna in friendship. When he returned home, he found his modest dwelling transformed into a beautiful home, his family gently provided for, his humility and affection intact, and the world a little kinder than before.

stories.title: Krishna Lifts Kaliya's Burden
body: Near Vrindavana, a many-hooded serpent named Kaliya had poisoned a pool of the Yamuna River, turning its waters into a place of fear for cows, birds, and villagers. The riverbank grew quiet, and no one dared to drink or bathe where the dark coils glimmered beneath the surface.

One day Krishna waded into the Yamuna and rose upon Kaliya's hoods, dancing lightly until the serpent's pride and venom finally broke. Hearing his wives praying for their husband's life, Krishna granted them mercy and told Kaliya to take his family to the ocean, where Garuda would no longer threaten him.

Kaliya and his household departed the river, and the Yamuna ran clean and safe once more. When Krishna returned to the cowherds on the bank, their faces lit with joy, and the village beside the holy water breathed easily again.

stories.title: The Jackal Who Found His Meal
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: A hungry jackal wandered near an old battlefield, where the wind moved through the hollow grass and dust. From far away came a sound so deep and thunderous that he trembled, picturing some great beast hiding behind the stones.

Yet his empty belly pushed him forward along the trail of that booming noise, until he came upon a tree whose branches struck a forgotten war-drum left behind from some past campaign. With careful claws he tore the drum open, certain that meat must lie within.

Inside he found only a scrap of dried skin, a modest meal instead of the feast he had feared, yet he had lived to eat it. Walking home lighter in step, the jackal carried a gentler wisdom: the loudest terrors often hold no danger for a brave and patient heart.

stories.title: The Ascetic's Gentle Treasure
stories.source: Mahakanha Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: High in a quiet hermitage, the ascetic Mahakanha was approached by Sakka, king of the devas, who asked if he would trade his simple life for worldly rule. Calmly, the sage answered that he prized harmlessness, patience, and generosity above any throne, for anger and greed make even mighty rulers restless and afraid.

Moved by the answer, Sakka revealed his radiant form and praised the wisdom of choosing a peaceful heart over power. Mahakanha smiled, knowing he had not won a contest but simply shared a truth. The treasure of virtue, he said, belongs to every willing soul, and the gods rejoiced at the teaching.

With Sakka's blessing still warm around him, Mahakanha returned to his gentle practice beneath the trees, his spirit steady and unafraid. The forest seemed to hum with quiet joy, and the simple path of compassion shone brighter than any crown ever could.
